00-header.heading: Did the ad beat the PSA?
00-header.text: 01 Marketing A/B Testing Analysis Data Analytics / Experimentation / BI Did the ad beat the PSA? Users shown the ad converted at 2.55% vs 1.79% for a PSA control: +0.77 percentage points (95% CI +0.60 to +0.94, p < 0.001) across 588,101 users. SQL · Tableau · Python GitHub

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: 588,101 Users analysed (one row per user) 2.55% vs 1.79% Ad vs PSA control conversion +0.77 pp Absolute lift, 95% CI +0.60 to +0.94 pp p = 1.7×10⁻¹³ Two-proportion z-test, z = 7.37

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: A marketing team has to decide whether to continue or expand an ad campaign. Two raw percentages are not enough, so I asked three questions. Do users shown the ad convert at a higher rate than a Public Service Announcement (PSA) control group? By how much? How certain is that estimate? I also kept statistical evidence separate from financial value. Answer: the ad group converted 0.77 percentage points more than the PSA control (95% CI +0.60 to +0.94), so I recommend continuing with monitoring, conditional on confirming how users were assigned and measuring real cost and margin.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Public Marketing A/B Testing dataset (Kaggle) Grain One row per user Size 588,101 users; six analytical fields: user ID, test group, converted, total ads, peak-exposure weekday, peak-exposure hour Ad group 564,577 users; 14,423 conversions PSA control 23,524 users; 420 conversions Split Roughly 96% ad / 4% PSA Period None. The data has no date column, so the analysis uses weekday and peak-exposure hour, not a calendar timeline.

03-pipeline-sql-python-tableau.heading: Pipeline: SQL → Python → Tableau
03-pipeline-sql-python-tableau.text: 03 Pipeline: SQL → Python → Tableau SQL (MySQL) A repeatable staged load: raw CSV to staging table to normalised analysis table, with the converted field mapped to 1/0 and row-count checkpoints. Three analysis queries: conversion rate by group; cumulative conversions by hour using window functions partitioned by group; conversion rate by weekday with explicit Monday-to-Sunday ordering. Python pandas validation and cleaning, group conversion rates, a statsmodels two-proportion z-test with a Wald confidence interval, Matplotlib charts, and a labelled business scenario. The SQL group counts were cross-checked against pandas. Tableau A packaged dashboard in two pages: KPI tiles with a group comparison, and exposure-segment views by weekday and hour.

04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.heading: Data Quality: Found and Fixed
04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.text: 04 Data Quality: Found and Fixed Row-count checkpoints: the scripted MySQL load counts rows at staging and again after normalisation, and both checks report the full 588,101 users before any analysis ran. Validation: the saved output reports zero nulls, empty strings, duplicate rows and duplicate user IDs. Both groups, all 7 weekdays and all 24 hours are present. Exported index column dropped, going from 7 columns to 6. No dates: I did not invent a daily trend. Chart titles say day and hour mean peak ad exposure, not conversion time. Reporting units: very small p-values print as 0.000000, so I report them in scientific notation, and I keep percentage points separate from relative lift.

05-findings.heading: Findings
05-findings.text: 05 Findings Ad group converted at 2.5547% (14,423 of 564,577). PSA control converted at 1.7854% (420 of 23,524). Absolute lift is +0.77 percentage points. Relative to the PSA baseline that is +43.1%. These are different quantities and are labelled separately. Two-sided two-proportion z-test: z = 7.37, p = 1.7×10⁻¹³. The 95% Wald confidence interval for the difference is +0.595 to +0.943 pp. Exposure is close between the groups: 24.82 ads per user in the ad group against 24.76 in the PSA group, with medians of 13 and 12. A rank-based test still flags a statistically detectable difference, so the groups are not perfectly balanced. Exploratory segments by peak-exposure weekday: Saturday has the lowest ad conversion rate (about 2.13%); Tuesday has the largest ad-vs-PSA gap (about +1.60 pp); Thursday has the smallest (about +0.14 pp); the Thursday and Sunday intervals include zero. No multiple-comparison correction was applied across the 31 day-and-hour comparisons (7 weekdays and 24 hours), and hours 3 to 6 each have fewer than 100 PSA users. These are hypotheses to test, not targeting rules. By peak-exposure hour, the ad rate is ahead in 23 of the 24 hours; the exception, hour 3, rests on one PSA conversion among 89 users.

07-method-and-validation.heading: Method and Validation
07-method-and-validation.text: 07 Method and Validation Null hypothesis: both groups have the same conversion proportion. The test is two-sided, using successes of 14,423 and 420 and sample sizes of 564,577 and 23,524. It assumes independent users, which the unique-user-ID check supports; it cannot confirm how users were assigned to groups. The confidence interval gives a range of plausible effect sizes. The p-value does not say whether the effect is large or profitable.

08-recommendation-and-impact.heading: Recommendation and Impact
08-recommendation-and-impact.text: 08 Recommendation and Impact Continue or expand the campaign with monitoring, conditional on confirming how users were assigned and measuring real cost and margin. Scenario, not a result: if the observed gap applied to the 564,577 ad-group users, that is about 4,343 additional conversions. At an assumed ₹500 order value, that is about ₹21.7 lakh (₹2,171,491) in gross value. Across the 95% confidence interval, the same scenario spans about ₹16.8 to ₹26.6 lakh. The data has no ad spend, margin or verified order values, so this is neither profit nor ROI.

09-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
09-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 09 Limitations and Next Steps The assignment mechanism is undocumented, so the lift is not proven causal. The roughly 96/4 split has no known intended ratio, so sample-ratio mismatch cannot be checked. There is no cost, margin or verified order value. There are no timestamps. Segment comparisons are exploratory. Next steps: a pre-specified segment plan, an alternative interval method as a robustness check, and a financial model built on real cost data.

00-header.heading: Can store-level sales be forecast well enough to plan with?
00-header.text: 02 Rossmann Store Sales Forecasting Data Analytics / Machine Learning / BI Can store-level sales be forecast well enough to plan with? XGBoost forecast chain-wide daily sales at 6.72% MAPE on an 84-day holdout, against 32.89% for Prophet at the same grain; the next 12 weeks total about 571.2 million in expected sales across 1,115 stores. SQL · Excel · Power BI · Python GitHub

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: 6.72% Chain-wide daily MAPE, XGBoost 32.89% Chain-wide daily MAPE, Prophet 12.93% Store-day MAPE, production XGBoost 571.2M Expected sales, next 84 days

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: Retail sales move with weekday, promotions, holidays, season and store characteristics. A forecast of the next 12 weeks can inform broad staffing and inventory-capacity planning: overestimating can mean excess labour or stock, underestimating can mean shortfalls. I built a store-level forecast for the 12 weeks after the data ends, compared two forecasting approaches on a time-ordered holdout, and presented the results in Power BI. No operational outcome or cost saving was measured, so the forecast is a planning proxy. Answer: the production model forecasts the next 84 days for all 1,115 stores, with an average percentage error of 6.72% on chain-wide daily sales and 12.93% on store-day sales; whether the forecast improves staffing or stock decisions was not tested.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Rossmann Store Sales competition data (Kaggle) Grain One row per store per day Size 1,017,209 store-days for 1,115 stores, 2013-01-01 to 2015-07-31 Tables A daily sales table (sales, customers, open, promo and holiday flags) and a store table (store type, assortment, competition and recurring-promotion fields) Modelling set 844,338 open, positive-sales store-days Holdout 2015-05-09 to 2015-07-31 (84 days): 766,584 training rows and 77,754 validation rows Forecast 2015-08-01 to 2015-10-23 (84 days) for 1,115 stores: 93,660 store-days Currency The data gives no currency; Rossmann operates in Germany, so figures are probably euros. Not in the data Product-level sales, prices, inventory, profit, future promotion schedules and future closure calendars

03-pipeline-sql-excel-python-power-bi.heading: Pipeline: SQL → Excel → Python → Power BI
03-pipeline-sql-excel-python-power-bi.text: 03 Pipeline: SQL → Excel → Python → Power BI SQL (MySQL) A relational schema (a store table and a train table keyed by store and date, with a foreign key), a load script that turns blank numeric fields into NULL, and seven query scripts: a filtered join, five analytical summaries (monthly sales by store type, per-store promo lift, top and bottom stores by revenue, month-over-month growth using LAG, seasonality by calendar month) and a full-data export. Excel Preliminary pivot analysis (monthly totals, store-type averages) for a first profile. Later measures use average sales per open store-day, because monthly totals mix the number of open days with sales intensity. Python Notebook 1 cleans and explores the data (imputation, row filtering, calendar features, six charts). Notebook 2 runs the Prophet and XGBoost experiments, the date-based validation, the production forecast and the saved models. Power BI A four-page report on a star schema: a date dimension and three fact tables (history, validation predictions, future forecast), with eleven DAX measures.

04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.heading: Data Quality: Found and Fixed
04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.text: 04 Data Quality: Found and Fixed Blank competition distances imported as zeros, which would have looked like a competitor at distance zero. The final load script converts blanks to NULL. Three missing competition distances were filled with the median across unique stores (2,325.0), not the row-weighted median (2,330.0), because the store table has one row per store. Removed 172,817 closed store-days and 54 open days with zero sales, leaving 844,338. Competition-open and Promo2 timing fields that are blank because they do not apply were left missing, not imputed. Added Month, Year and WeekOfYear, and one-hot encoded store type, assortment and promo interval, using the same encoding at forecast time.

05-exploratory-findings.heading: Exploratory Findings
05-exploratory-findings.text: 05 Exploratory Findings Store type B has the highest average sales per open store-day (about 10.2K, against 6.8K to 6.9K for the other types), but it has only 17 stores and differs in assortment and opening pattern. This is descriptive, not a type effect. Promo days average higher sales in 1,114 of 1,115 stores. Promotion assignment is not random, so this is an association, not a causal lift. Saturday is the weakest weekday per open store-day (about 5.9K); Monday and Sunday are the highest (about 8.2K each). Sunday looks strong per open store but weak chain-wide, because few stores open. December has the highest average sales per open store-day (about 8.6K, against about 6.5K to 7.2K in other months), but the data contains only two Decembers, so seasonal certainty is limited. Competition distance has no simple relationship with average store sales. The highest-selling stores sit at short distances, which may reflect dense, high-traffic locations and not a competitor effect.

06-model-comparison.heading: Model Comparison
06-model-comparison.text: 06 Model Comparison Prophet, baseline 63.76% chain-wide daily MAPE (MAE 857,491; RMSE 1,418,151) Prophet, German public holidays 32.89% (MAE 607,088; RMSE 920,710). Kept as the Prophet comparator. Prophet, tuned 22.48% MAPE, but MAE 662,991 and RMSE 968,381 are both worse than the holiday-aware model, so it was not selected. Three settings changed together, so the cause is not isolated. XGBoost, chain-wide daily 6.72% (MAE 409,790; RMSE 617,347) for the production model. XGBoost, store-day 21.00% default; 17.92% after manual tuning; 12.64% with Promo and a store-level baseline (not usable, no future Promo schedule); 12.93% production without Promo (MAE 839; RMSE 1,138). Prophet + XGBoost blends 50/50: 17.99%. 80/20 toward XGBoost: 10.20%. XGBoost alone: 6.72%. Prophet did not improve the chain-wide forecast. Like for like: XGBoost store-day predictions were summed by date and compared with Prophet on chain-wide daily totals (6.72% against 32.89%). The 12.93% store-day figure answers a harder, different question and is not compared with Prophet. Production XGBoost leaves out Promo because future promotions are unknown. The same 84-day holdout was used to choose between variants, so the scores are mildly optimistic. The randomised search (15 combinations, date-grouped expanding-window folds) selected n_estimators=200 and max_depth=6.

07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.heading: Mistakes I Caught and Corrected
07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.text: 07 Mistakes I Caught and Corrected Mismatched grain: my first comparison put Prophet's chain-wide daily score next to XGBoost's store-day score. Summing XGBoost predictions by date made it like for like: 32.89% against 6.72%. Wrong validation split: an early split took the last 84 rows, not the last 84 dates across all stores. A date mask replaced it, giving 766,584 training and 77,754 validation rows. Prophet error diagnosis: a 63.76% MAPE looked like general failure, but sorting the errors showed the worst days (May 14 and May 25, 2015) were near-total closures (97.1% and 97.0% of stores closed). Adding a German public-holiday calendar brought MAPE to 32.89%. Weekday encoding: training weekdays ran 1 to 7 while pandas uses 0 to 6, which would have shifted future-date features by a day. I aligned them and added assertions in Notebook 2. Dashboard scatter: it collapsed to four store-type points because it had no store identifier. A per-store category restored one point per store. Overclaims withdrawn: March and July month-over-month changes (March 2014 +7.88%, July 2014 -8.50%) are not a recurring seasonal lift; Sunday is not the weakest day (it is low chain-wide because stores are closed); and promotions do not help every store, since one store shows a negative lift.

PredictedSales is the estimate if the store is open. ExpectedSales multiplies it by OpenRate, the store's historical share of open days for that weekday. Expected sales over the 84 days: 571,208,572. Sanity check, not validation: for the 931 stores that traded normally over the same 84 days of 2014, expected 2015 sales are 480.2M against 451.0M actual in 2014 (+6.5%). 10-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
10-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 10 Limitations and Next Steps The production model gives point estimates only, with no prediction intervals. The data spans about 2.6 years, so annual seasonality is weakly supported. The 84-day holdout was reused to choose between variants and there is no untouched test period, so the scores are mildly optimistic. There is no future promotion schedule, so Promo is excluded from the production model. OpenRate is a weekday-level historical average. It does not model closure schedules or public-holiday closures. No business impact was measured. The repository's Query 7 export is incomplete (48,328 of 1,017,209 rows); Notebook 1 reads the separate full merged file. The raw competition CSVs are not committed. Next steps: an untouched test period or rolling-origin evaluation; known calendar, closure or promotion data only if available at forecast time; prediction intervals; and measuring operational value once a forecast is used.

00-header.heading: Who is leaving, and where should retention focus?
00-header.text: 03 Banking Churn Analysis Data Analytics / SQL / BI Who is leaving, and where should retention focus? Across 10,127 credit card customers, 16.07% churned. Churners made far fewer transactions (44.9 against 68.7), and attrition jumps from 12.49% at two contacts in the last 12 months to 20.15% at three. SQL · Power BI · Python GitHub

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: 16.07% Attrition rate, 1,627 of 10,127 customers $13.24M Credit limits on churned accounts -0.37 Correlation of transaction count with churn 12.49% → 20.15% Attrition at 2 vs 3 contacts in the last 12 months

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: A credit card issuer loses interchange and interest income when customers leave, and churn often shows up as disengagement before an account closes. I analysed 10,127 customers to answer three questions for a retention team: which segments churn, which behaviours separate churned from retained customers, and where retention effort should focus. I kept the work diagnostic and transparent, with no predictive model, so every rule can be audited in SQL, Python and Power BI. Answer: churn concentrates among customers whose transactions are low, who use little of their credit limit, and who reach three or more contacts in the last 12 months (attrition rises from 12.49% at two contacts to 20.15% at three), so retention effort should start there; these are associations to test, not proven causes.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Credit Card Customers dataset (Kaggle) Grain One row per customer Size 10,127 customers; 23 raw columns, 20 after cleaning Target 1,627 attrited customers (16.07%) and 8,500 existing customers Fields Demographics (age, gender, dependents, education, marital status, income band), card tier, relationship length and product count, and 12-month behaviour (transactions, inactive months, contacts in the last 12 months, utilisation, revolving balance, credit limit, quarter-over-quarter change) Limit A single snapshot: 12-month aggregates, with no dates and no account-closure timestamps

03-pipeline-sql-python-power-bi.heading: Pipeline: SQL → Python → Power BI
03-pipeline-sql-python-power-bi.text: 03 Pipeline: SQL → Python → Power BI SQL (MySQL) Seven query scripts: overall attrition rate (with a window function), attrition by card tier, behaviour of churned versus retained customers, the top 50 churned accounts by credit limit (a CTE with ROW_NUMBER), attrition by income band, spend-velocity change, and attrition by number of contacts in the last 12 months. Python A 14-cell notebook (12 code cells and 2 markdown cells) using pandas, matplotlib and seaborn for cleaning, data-quality checks, seven charts and a 15×15 correlation matrix. Power BI A three-page report (Executive Overview, Behavioural Signals, At-Risk Profiles) whose visuals are driven by 13 DAX measures over three tables: the cleaned customer table and two SQL result tables. Cross-check Six quantities, each traced below to the file, notebook cell or visual that computes it. Recomputed means the tool derives the figure from the data it holds; checked against the SQL export means it reads the exported result. Customer counts: MySQL counts them in sql/01_attrition_rate.sql, which groups the raw import by attrition flag; pandas prints them in notebook cells 2 and 3, before and after the leakage columns are dropped; Power BI recomputes them in the "Total Customers" card on Executive Overview, a DAX measure over the cleaned table. Attrition rate: MySQL computes it in sql/01_attrition_rate.sql, a window function over the raw import; pandas computes it in notebook cell 6, which prints the share of attrited customers; Power BI recomputes it in the attrition-rate card and the attrition-by-card-tier bar chart on Executive Overview, both DAX measures over the cleaned table. Card-tier rates: MySQL computes them in sql/02_attrition_by_card.sql, a CTE over the raw import; pandas computes them in notebook cell 7, which groups the cleaned table by card tier; Power BI recomputes them in the attrition-by-card-tier bar chart on Executive Overview, the "Attrition Rate" measure over the cleaned table. Behaviour averages: MySQL computes them in sql/03_behavioral_comparison.sql and sql/06_spend_decline.sql; pandas computes them in notebook cells 8, 9, 10 and 12, the boxplots, the spend-versus-frequency scatter and the utilisation means; Power BI recomputes them in the three Behavioural Signals average charts and the spend-decline chart on At-Risk Profiles, DAX measures over the cleaned table, while the scatter reads the raw columns. Contact-bucket rates: MySQL computes them in sql/07_contacts_vs_attrition.sql, with 5 and 6 contacts merged into a "5+" bucket; pandas does not compute them; Power BI does not recompute them either, because the bucket chart on At-Risk Profiles reads the query7 SQL export, so those figures were checked against the SQL export instead. Churned credit exposure: MySQL does not compute it and pandas does not compute it; Power BI recomputes it in the "Credit Exposure" card on Executive Overview, a DAX measure over the cleaned table.

04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.heading: Data Quality: Found and Fixed
04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.text: 04 Data Quality: Found and Fixed Target leakage: the raw file includes two columns of probabilities from a Naive Bayes model already fitted on the churn label. I excluded them. Their 130-character names also broke the MySQL import, whose column-name limit is 64 characters. Hidden missing values: there are no nulls, but "Unknown" strings stand in for missing education (15.00%), income (10.98%) and marital status (7.40%), and 3,046 customers (30.08%) have at least one. I kept "Unknown" as its own category instead of dropping almost a third of the data or imputing labels. Churn in those groups (16.82% to 17.22%) is close to the portfolio rate of 16.07%. Credit-limit ceiling: 508 customers (5.02%) share exactly $34,516.00 and 507 share $1,438.30, and both groups average 36.0 months as customers, which is consistent with capping in the source data. It surfaced when RANK() returned 89 tied rows instead of 50 for the top churned accounts. ROW_NUMBER() with a tie-break on transaction amount fixed the ranking. Small cell: all 54 customers with 6 contacts in the last 12 months churned, which would distort a chart. I merged 5 and 6 contacts into a "5+" bucket (113 of 230, 49.13%) and kept the 54-customer finding in the notes.

05-findings.heading: Findings
05-findings.text: 05 Findings 1,627 of 10,127 customers churned (16.07%). Their accounts held $13.24M in credit limits (mean $8,136). That is credit exposure, not lost revenue. Transaction count is the strongest signal: churned customers averaged 44.93 transactions against 68.67 for retained customers (median 43 vs 71; correlation -0.37). The most transactions any churned customer made was 94, against 139 for retained customers. Contacts in the last 12 months show a cliff: attrition is 1.75% at 0 contacts, 7.20% at 1, 12.49% at 2, 20.15% at 3, 22.63% at 4 and 49.13% at 5 or more (230 customers). Low utilisation: churned customers averaged 16.25% credit utilisation against 29.64% for retained customers. Among the 50 churned accounts the top-50 query returns — ranked by credit limit, with the ties broken by transaction amount — 20 had no revolving balance and the group averaged 2.15% utilisation. Ranking by credit limit alone, with those ties unresolved, returns 24 instead, so the ordering is what fixes the count. Spending contracted more for churners: the Q4-to-Q1 transaction-count ratio averaged 0.554 against 0.742, and the spend ratio 0.694 against 0.773. Both groups are below 1.0, so the signal is the size of the drop, not the direction. Blue cards hold 93.36% of churned customers (1,519 of 1,627). Platinum has the highest rate (25.00%) but on only 20 customers, and Gold is 18.10% on 116, so those are small-sample results, not findings to act on. Income shows no clear gradient: among known income bands, attrition runs from 13.48% to 17.33%, with the top band (17.33%) and the under-$40K band (17.19%) highest. Age, dependents and time as a customer each correlate with churn at about 0.02 or less.

06-recommendations.heading: Recommendations
06-recommendations.text: 06 Recommendations Route accounts to a retention specialist once they reach 3 or more contacts in the last 12 months. Flag accounts whose yearly transaction count is falling towards 45, the leavers' average. Target customers with zero or very low utilisation and 2 to 3 or more inactive months with incentives such as cashback or balance transfers. Do not launch a Platinum-wide campaign on 20 customers; review those accounts individually. These are starting points to test, not measured savings or validated thresholds. The data is a single snapshot with no costs and no record of any retention action.

07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.heading: Mistakes I Caught and Corrected
07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.text: 07 Mistakes I Caught and Corrected A trap in the card breakdown: Blue cards hold 1,519 of the 1,627 churners, which looks like a Blue problem. But Blue is 93% of all customers and its 16.10% churn rate matches the 16.07% overall. Platinum has the highest rate (25.00%), but on 20 customers (5 churners), too few to act on. The behavioural signal is activity: leavers averaged 44.9 transactions a year against 68.7 for stayers, a gap of 23.7. I first labelled the $13.24M "Revenue at Risk." A credit limit is the most a bank allows a customer to borrow, not revenue, so I renamed it "Credit Exposure." A dashboard note said "about 508 attrited customers" sit at the credit-limit ceiling. 508 is all customers at the ceiling; 89 of them are attrited. I corrected the note. The Power BI top-50 table sorted by customer ID instead of the transaction-amount order from SQL. I set the sort in the visual. Spend-trend label: my SQL labelled both churned and retained customers "Declining Spend," because both averages are below 1.0. I kept the query as it was and changed the interpretation, not the threshold. Power BI display bugs: KPI cards abbreviated 10,127 to "10K" (fixed with a DAX FORMAT measure), and the "5+" contact bucket lost its "+" because Power Query typed the column as a number (fixed by setting it to text). Self-audit fixes: I committed the seven SQL scripts the README referred to, replaced an absolute notebook path with a relative one, and saved the notebook's executed outputs.

10-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
10-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 10 Limitations and Next Steps The data is a single snapshot with no dates or closure timestamps, so I cannot measure how long before closing a third service contact occurs, and the findings are associations, not causes. The analysis uses group means, boxplots and correlations, with no hypothesis tests or multivariate controls. Credit limits appear capped at both ends in the source data (508 customers at $34,516.00 and 507 at $1,438.30), so credit-limit findings need care. Platinum (20 customers) and Gold (116) rates are unstable, and the 6-contact group (54 customers) is merged into "5+". Credit exposure is a total of credit limits, not revenue, cost or profit. Next steps: Welch t-tests, Mann-Whitney U and chi-square tests with confidence intervals (Wilson intervals for the small card tiers), then a leakage-free predictive model (regularised logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees) evaluated with stratified cross-validation and precision-recall AUC, with explainability.

00-header.heading: Where is revenue high but profit thin?
00-header.text: 04 Retail Sales Analysis Data Analytics / BI Where is revenue high but profit thin? Across 9,994 Sample Superstore order lines (2014–2017), Furniture earned $742K in sales at a 2.49% margin while Tables, Bookcases and Supplies lost money, shown in Python charts and a Power BI report. Power BI · Python GitHub

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: $2.30M Total sales, 9,994 order lines 12.47% Overall profit margin ($286.4K profit) 2.49% Furniture margin, against 17.40% for Technology 3 of 17 Sub-categories with negative profit

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: Raw transaction rows are hard for a business team to read, and high sales do not guarantee healthy profit. One order can hold several line items, so counting rows overstates orders. I analysed the Sample Superstore data to separate revenue from profit quality: which categories, sub-categories, regions and months drive sales, and where margin is thin or negative. I then packaged the answers in a Power BI report that a manager can filter by region. The work is descriptive: it points to where to investigate, not to what caused a loss. Answer: revenue and profit quality diverge. Technology and Office Supplies keep about 17% of sales as profit, Furniture keeps 2.49%, and Tables, Bookcases and Supplies lose money; the Power BI report lets a manager filter these views by region, and the next step is to investigate the causes.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Sample Superstore retail dataset (public Kaggle and Tableau Community distribution) Grain One row per order line item; a single order can have several lines Size 9,994 line items from 5,009 distinct orders and 793 customers, in 21 raw columns Period Orders dated 2014-01-03 to 2017-12-30 Quality 0 missing values and 0 duplicate rows in the 21 raw columns Derived Five added columns (order year, order month, month name, weekday and shipping duration), making 26 columns; shipping took 0 to 7 days, about 3.96 on average

03-pipeline-python-power-bi.heading: Pipeline: Python → Power BI
03-pipeline-python-power-bi.text: 03 Pipeline: Python → Power BI Python Read the raw file with the correct Windows-1252 encoding, checked shape, types, missing values and duplicates, parsed the dates, added the calendar and shipping columns, wrote a prepared CSV and exported six charts at 300 DPI. Power BI A report built on that prepared CSV, with a region slicer, KPI cards, profit by sub-category, a state map, sales by category and a calendar-month sales chart. DAX Three explicit measures: Total Revenue, Total Profit and Total Orders. Total Orders uses DISTINCTCOUNT of Order ID, so an order with several lines counts once. Handoff The prepared CSV is the data contract between Python and Power BI.

04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.heading: Data Quality: Found and Fixed
04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.text: 04 Data Quality: Found and Fixed Encoding: the raw CSV failed to load as UTF-8 (a UnicodeDecodeError). I specified Windows-1252 instead of dropping characters. Rows are not orders: 9,994 rows are order lines, not orders. I report 9,994 line items and 5,009 distinct orders separately, and the Power BI order count uses DISTINCTCOUNT. 05-findings.text: 05 Findings Total sales are $2,297,200.86 and total profit is $286,397.02, an overall margin of 12.47%. 00-header.heading: Which telecom customers are likely to leave?
00-header.text: 05 Customer Churn Prediction Machine Learning / Classification Which telecom customers are likely to leave? Logistic Regression, chosen by cross-validated ROC-AUC (0.8463 against 0.8455 for Random Forest, effectively a tie), flags 77.81% of churners among 1,407 held-out telecom customers (test ROC-AUC 0.8310) and runs in a live Streamlit app. Python · scikit-learn · Streamlit GitHub Live application

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: 0.8310 Test ROC-AUC, Logistic Regression 77.81% Logistic Regression churn recall on 1,407 held-out customers 49.91% Logistic Regression precision at the 0.50 threshold 42.7% vs 2.8% Churn: month-to-month vs two-year contracts

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: A telecom company wants to spot customers likely to leave and estimate churn risk for a given customer profile. I used a public sample of 7,043 customers to ask how common churn is, how it varies with contract, tenure, charges and services, and whether a classifier can separate churners from stayers on customers it has not seen well enough to score one customer at a time in a web app. The result is a decision-support prototype, not a live retention system, and I treated every pattern as an association. Answer: a Logistic Regression model scores a customer's churn risk and catches 77.81% of churners on held-out customers, at the cost of about two flagged customers for every real churner; the project does not test whether retention offers work.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source IBM Telco Customer Churn sample (Kaggle) Grain One row per customer Size 7,043 rows × 21 columns; 5,174 stayed and 1,869 churned (26.5%) After cleaning 7,032 rows × 20 columns: 11 blank TotalCharges records removed and customerID dropped Model input 36 ordered predictors after encoding and adding five engineered features Split Stratified 80/20: 5,625 training customers and 1,407 test customers Limit One public dataset with no dates, so performance on other customers or later periods is unknown

03-pipeline.heading: Pipeline
03-pipeline.text: 03 Pipeline Cleaning Converted TotalCharges to numeric (11 blank strings became missing and were dropped), removed customerID, mapped Churn to 0 and 1, and one-hot encoded the categorical fields. Features Five engineered features: tenure group (new up to 12 months, mid 13 to 48, loyal 49 to 72), a count of eight services, a new-customer flag, average monthly charge from total charges, and a high-value flag for monthly charges above 70.60, the training-row median. Validation Scaling and then SMOTE were applied inside each of five cross-validation folds, and the test set was never resampled. After SMOTE the training data has 8,260 rows. Models Logistic Regression and Random Forest, compared on mean 5-fold cross-validated ROC-AUC. App A Streamlit form that engineers the same features, aligns the encoded columns to the saved training schema, scales the row, and returns churn and retention probabilities, a risk band and example outreach suggestions. Tests pytest checks for tenure-group boundaries and for parity between batch and single-customer feature encoding.

04-findings.heading: Findings
04-findings.text: 04 Findings Churn is 26.5% (1,869 of 7,043), so a model that always predicts "stay" would look about 73.5% accurate while catching no churners. Contract is the strongest pattern: churn is 42.7% on month-to-month contracts, 11.3% on one-year and 2.8% on two-year. This is an association; contract type may be tied to tenure, price or service mix. Churners had a median tenure of 10 months against 38 for customers who stayed. Churn is 47.68% for new customers (12 months or less), 23.64% for mid and 9.51% for loyal. Churners paid more per month on average ($74.44 against $61.31), which may reflect contract and service mix as well as price. Correlations with churn: tenure -0.35, fiber optic internet +0.31, two-year contract -0.30, electronic check payment +0.30. Churn by number of services is uneven: 43.8% with none, 21.2% with one, 36.5% with three, falling to 5.3% with all eight.

05-model-comparison.heading: Model Comparison
05-model-comparison.text: 05 Model Comparison Logistic Regression (selected) Mean 5-fold CV ROC-AUC 0.8463. Held-out test: ROC-AUC 0.8310, accuracy 73.35%, precision 49.91%, recall 77.81%, F1 0.6082. Random Forest Mean 5-fold CV ROC-AUC 0.8455. Held-out test: ROC-AUC 0.8344, accuracy 76.69%, precision 54.83%, recall 69.79%, F1 0.6141. Everyone-stays baseline Labelling every held-out customer "stay" is 73.42% accurate (1,033 of 1,407), and Logistic Regression's 73.35% accuracy is no better than doing nothing. So accuracy is not the number to read here; recall is: Logistic Regression catches 77.81% of churners, against 69.79% for Random Forest, whose 76.69% accuracy comes with fewer churners caught. Why Logistic Regression It was selected on the cross-validation criterion. Random Forest scores slightly higher on the test set, but test results do not override the selection rule. Errors, Logistic Regression Of 374 churners in the test set, 291 were caught and 83 missed; of 1,033 stayers, 292 were flagged by mistake. The margin is small: the cross-validated AUC lead is 0.0008, and I did not run repeated splits or report fold-to-fold variation, so another seed could change the choice. At a 0.50 threshold about half of the flagged customers are real churners (precision 49.91%), so a retention team would contact about two customers for every one who would leave.

06-how-a-retention-team-could-use-this.heading: How a Retention Team Could Use This
06-how-a-retention-team-could-use-this.text: 06 How a Retention Team Could Use This Review customers in the high-risk band (above 0.70) first. Look first at month-to-month contracts (42.7% churn) and at customers in their first 12 months (47.68% churn), and test annual-contract offers there. Read the probabilities as relative risk, not an exact chance of leaving, because they are not calibrated. These are suggestions to test, not measured outcomes: the project does not test whether retention offers work.

07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.heading: Mistakes I Caught and Corrected
07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.text: 07 Mistakes I Caught and Corrected Blank TotalCharges escaped my missing-value check because empty strings are not NaN. I coerced the column to numeric and dropped the 11 rows; all 11 had tenure zero. Encoding mismatch at prediction time: one-hot encoding a single customer with drop_first removed the only category present, so the row no longer matched the training columns. I now create every category, reindex to the saved ordered feature list and fill missing columns with zero. A recorded review estimated the old behaviour shifted the mean predicted churn probability by 20.48 percentage points and changed 1,566 of 7,032 predictions; I treat that as a historical estimate, not a rerun result. Leakage in a feature threshold: I first computed the high-value cutoff on the full dataset, so test data influenced a feature. It is now computed from training rows only and stored for the app. Cross-validation did not match final training: validation used different scaling, and SMOTE's neighbour search ran on unscaled features. I moved scaling before SMOTE inside every fold. Model selection overwritten: the test-set winner had replaced the cross-validation choice in the saved model label. I kept the cross-validation choice as the selected model and marked the test winner as informational. Tenure boundaries differed between training and the app. I standardised them (new up to 12, mid 13 to 48, loyal above 48) and added boundary tests. Risk bands versus predicted class: the app's bands (low up to 0.40, medium up to 0.70, high above 0.70) differ from the 0.50 class threshold, so a medium badge can come with a "stay" prediction. The app now explains this.

08-the-live-app.heading: The Live App
08-the-live-app.text: 08 The Live App The Streamlit app takes one customer profile (tenure 1 to 72 months, monthly charges $0 to $150, total charges $0 to $10,000) and returns churn and retention probabilities, a risk band, a probability chart and example outreach actions. The suggested actions are static examples, not validated interventions, and the probabilities are not calibrated.

10-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
10-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 10 Limitations and Next Steps The data is one public dataset with a single 80/20 split, so performance on other customers or later periods is unknown. Probabilities are not calibrated, because SMOTE changes the training class balance; read them as relative risk, not an exact chance of leaving. The 0.50 threshold and the 0.40 and 0.70 risk bands were not chosen from a retention cost or capacity analysis. Logistic Regression's cross-validated lead is only 0.0008, and robustness across seeds and repeated splits is not shown. There is no subgroup or fairness assessment. The notebook still computes the engineered features inline, duplicating the module the app uses, so the two can drift. No financial impact is claimed: the project does not test a retention campaign or estimate customer value. Next steps: report fold-to-fold variation and repeated-split results, tie the threshold to a retention budget, check calibration and subgroup performance, and have training and the app import the same feature code.

00-header.heading: Do food reviews agree with their star ratings?
00-header.text: 06 Product Review Sentiment Analysis NLP / Sentiment Analysis Do food reviews agree with their star ratings? Across 568,454 Amazon food reviews, VADER agrees with a star-rating proxy on 80.38% of reviews and labels 49.47% of one-star reviews positive: a lexicon-based workflow with a Plotly dashboard and a Streamlit app. Python · VADER · Plotly · Streamlit GitHub Live application

00-metrics.heading: 00-metrics
00-metrics.text: 568,454 Amazon food reviews analysed 88.21% Reviews VADER labels positive 80.38% Agreement vs a 78.07% always-positive baseline (not accuracy) 49.47% One-star reviews VADER labels positive

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: A star rating squeezes a whole review into one number, and nobody can read half a million comments. I wanted to know whether practical text-analysis methods can summarise a large review collection: how the language labels relate to star ratings, which products and years show higher negative shares, and which phrases rank highly in each group. The project is descriptive. It does not train a classifier, and I treat star ratings as a rough proxy for sentiment, not as ground truth. Answer: as a first-pass summary, yes, with limits: VADER labels 88.21% of reviews positive and agrees with a star-rating proxy on 80.38%, but it labels 49.47% of one-star reviews positive, so its labels need human checks before decisions.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Amazon Fine Food Reviews (Stanford SNAP collection) Grain One row per review Size 568,454 reviews × 10 raw columns (about 300.9 MB); 17 columns in the processed file Period 8 October 1999 to 26 October 2012 Ratings 1 star: 52,268; 2 stars: 29,769; 3 stars: 42,640; 4 stars: 80,655; 5 stars: 363,122 Missing 26 ProfileName and 27 Summary values; no other raw column has missing values Limit There are no human-labelled sentiment values, so star ratings are the only comparison label

03-pipeline.heading: Pipeline
03-pipeline.text: 03 Pipeline Cleaning Two text paths. For VADER: strip HTML first, then URLs, and normalise whitespace while keeping the capitalisation, punctuation and emoticons VADER reads. For word and phrase analysis: lowercase, expand negative contractions, remove punctuation and digits, tokenise, and drop stopwords except "not", "no" and "nor". Scoring VADER compound score from -1 to +1: at or above +0.05 is positive, at or below -0.05 is negative, and anything between is neutral. TextBlob polarity and subjectivity were computed as a comparison. Proxy Star ratings mapped to three classes: 1 to 2 stars negative, 3 stars neutral, 4 to 5 stars positive. Summaries Label mix by star rating, product, year and review length; word clouds; and TF-IDF phrases of two to three words from a balanced sample of 5,000 reviews per class. Outputs A processed CSV, saved charts, a five-panel Plotly HTML dashboard and a Streamlit app that scores one typed review.

04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.heading: Data Quality: Found and Fixed
04-data-quality-found-and-fixed.text: 04 Data Quality: Found and Fixed Cleaning that erased sentiment cues: aggressive cleaning removes the capitalisation, punctuation and negation that VADER reads, so I built a separate VADER path and kept "not", "no" and "nor" in the phrase path. HTML and URL order: removing URLs before HTML could swallow real words inside links, so I strip HTML first and added regression examples for links, negation and word corruption. Empty text read as neutral: a review that is empty after cleaning scores 0.0 and looks neutral, so I added a vader_empty flag and mark empty TextBlob results as missing. The current processed file has no such rows, but the guard stays. Fragile paths and schema: the notebook now finds the project root from either folder, uses a strict column drop and asserts the expected 17-column schema.

05-findings.heading: Findings
05-findings.text: 05 Findings VADER labels 501,419 reviews positive (88.21%), 55,646 negative (9.79%) and 11,389 neutral (2.00%). It agrees with the star-rating proxy on 80.38% of reviews, with 111,534 disagreements. That is agreement with a proxy, not accuracy against human-labelled sentiment. A baseline that labels every review positive would agree with the proxy on 78.07% (443,777 of 568,454, the four- and five-star reviews), so VADER's 80.38% is 2.3 points above that baseline, and TextBlob's 75.94% falls below it. Overall agreement hides the minority classes: from the confusion matrix, VADER matches the proxy on 95.2% of positive-proxy reviews but only 40.1% of negative-proxy and 3.8% of neutral-proxy reviews. VADER labels 49.47% of one-star reviews and 65.11% of two-star reviews positive, which shows a large mismatch between the text label and the rating. TextBlob agrees with the proxy on 75.94% (saved notebook output, not recomputable from the processed CSV), and mean TextBlob subjectivity is 0.5501. Among 5,030 products with at least 20 reviews, the highest VADER-negative share is 66.7% (16 of 24 reviews). That is a small-group share, not a quality verdict. Yearly positive share (years with at least 100 reviews, 2003 to 2012) runs from 86.27% in 2004 to 93.18% in 2003. These are descriptive differences, not causes. Positive reviews average 81.66 words, negative 75.69 and neutral 41.34. This is an association only. Top TF-IDF phrases overlap across classes: "not sure" and "grocery store" appear in the top phrases of more than one group, so a top phrase is not necessarily distinctive.

06-how-i-would-use-these-results.heading: How I Would Use These Results
06-how-i-would-use-these-results.text: 06 How I Would Use These Results Use VADER labels as a first-pass summary of a large review set, not as a verdict on any single review. Check low-rating reviews by hand: about half of one-star reviews get a positive text label. Compare products only above a minimum review count, and show the count next to every rate. Treat yearly and review-length differences as questions to investigate, not explanations. Measuring true sentiment accuracy would need a stratified, human-labelled sample, which this project does not have.

07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.heading: Mistakes I Caught and Corrected
07-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.text: 07 Mistakes I Caught and Corrected Agreement called accuracy: I first described agreement with star ratings as accuracy. Stars are not human-labelled sentiment and the three-way mapping loses information, so I renamed it "agreement with the star-rating proxy." A confidence label that was not confidence: the app showed the absolute VADER compound score times 100 as "Confidence," which reads like a probability. I renamed it "Score Magnitude" and explained that it measures distance from neutral. A neutral example that was not neutral: the app's example review scored -0.092, which is negative under my thresholds. I replaced it with one that scores 0.000 and tested the examples against the real scoring function. Product and yearly claims that changed: earlier output named different products and years and implied quality rankings. I recomputed from the processed table, applied minimum sizes (20 reviews per product, 100 per year) and relabelled the measure "negative-label share." Word-frequency overreach: removing negators and calling phrases "distinctive" misled readers, so I kept negators and now describe results as top within-group phrases. Streamlit failures: the app imported functions that did not exist yet, and its example buttons did not fill the text box because widget state was set in the wrong order. I aligned the module and initialised state first.

10-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
10-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 10 Limitations and Next Steps VADER and TextBlob are general lexicon methods and can miss sarcasm, mixed feelings and domain-specific language. Star ratings are an imperfect proxy, so 80.38% agreement is not accuracy. Positive reviews dominate (88.21%), so overall agreement can hide poor handling of negative reviews. Product and year summaries are descriptive and do not show product quality or causes. TextBlob's 75.94% comes from saved notebook output and cannot be recomputed from the processed CSV, which stores subjectivity but not polarity or labels. TF-IDF results depend on the 5,000-per-class sample, the cleaning and the settings. I have not shown a clean-machine rerun of the whole pipeline. Next steps: a stratified, human-labelled sample to measure true accuracy, exporting TextBlob polarity and labels so its agreement can be recomputed, one script that regenerates every output, and automated tests for the shared cleaner.

01-business-problem-and-decision.heading: Business Problem and Decision
01-business-problem-and-decision.text: 01 Business Problem and Decision The problem: Property prices are often judged by subjective comparisons or a single number such as price per unit of area, which ignores layout, stories, parking, road access and furnishing all at once. I used 545 houses to ask three questions: which attributes move with price, whether a tuned Random Forest beats a standardised linear baseline on a dataset this small, and whether the whole pipeline can be built cleanly enough to audit and reproduce. This is an analytical exercise, not a valuation tool. Answer: area, bathrooms and the engineered luxury score move most with price, a plain Linear Regression beat the tuned Random Forest on this split (test R² 0.6583 against 0.5977), and the pipeline is documented and audited.

02-data.heading: Data
02-data.text: 02 Data Source Housing Prices dataset (Kaggle) Grain One row per house Size 545 houses; 13 raw columns (price plus 12 attributes); 0 missing values and 0 duplicate rows Attributes Area, bedrooms, bathrooms, stories, parking, six yes/no features (main road, guest room, basement, hot water heating, air conditioning, preferred area) and furnishing status Units Price and area carry no currency or measurement unit in the source, so everything is reported in dataset units

03-pipeline.heading: Pipeline
03-pipeline.text: 03 Pipeline Cleaning Checked for missing values and duplicates, audited the categories of every text column, mapped six yes/no columns to 1 and 0, and one-hot encoded furnishing status, dropping one level to avoid a redundant dummy column. Features Three engineered features: bed_bath_count (bedrooms + bathrooms), area_per_bed_bath (area divided by that count) and luxury_score (a count of five amenities: air conditioning, hot water heating, preferred area, guest room, basement). Split and scaling An 80/20 split with a fixed seed: 436 training houses and 109 test houses. StandardScaler was fitted on the training rows only, so no test information leaks into training. Models Linear Regression on the scaled features, and a Random Forest tuned by 5-fold cross-validated grid search over 108 combinations (540 fits) on the training rows. Best forest: 100 trees, max depth 7, minimum 2 houses per leaf; best cross-validated R² 0.6351. Evaluation MAE, RMSE and R² for both models on the same 109 held-out houses, plus training scores to check for overfitting. Artifacts Both models and the scaler saved with joblib, with library versions pinned to match.

04-findings.heading: Findings
04-findings.text: 04 Findings Price is right-skewed: the mean is 4,766,729 against a median of 4,340,000 (skewness +1.21), with a tail up to 13,300,000. A log transform brings skewness down to +0.14. The strongest correlations with price are area (+0.54), bathrooms (+0.52), luxury_score (+0.51), bed_bath_count (+0.51) and air conditioning (+0.45). Unfurnished status is the one clear negative (-0.28). These are associations, not causes. Several features overlap: bed_bath_count correlates +0.89 with bedrooms and +0.75 with bathrooms, and luxury_score is built from five amenity columns. In the Random Forest, area carries 46.2% of the importance, and the three engineered features together carry 23.4%. In the linear model, area has the largest standardised coefficient: +946,722 per standard deviation of area. At a given area, unfurnished houses sit lower in price. This is descriptive. Both models underpredict the most expensive houses. The two test houses priced above 12 million (12.2M and 13.3M) were predicted at roughly 7M to 8.5M, which pushes RMSE well above MAE.

05-model-comparison.heading: Model Comparison
05-model-comparison.text: 05 Model Comparison Linear Regression Test R² 0.6583, MAE 966,320, RMSE 1,314,226. Training R² 0.6896, a gap of 0.0313. Random Forest, tuned Test R² 0.5977, MAE 1,049,055, RMSE 1,426,042. Training R² 0.8784, a gap of 0.2807, which is clear overfitting. Difference Linear Regression is better on all three test metrics: R² higher by 0.0606, MAE lower by 82,735 (7.89%) and RMSE lower by 111,816 (7.84%). Scale The linear model's average miss (MAE 966,320) is about 20% of the mean price (4,766,729). Why the linear model held up, as hypotheses I did not test: price rises fairly smoothly with area, bathrooms, stories and amenities; 436 training houses leave few houses per forest leaf, so deep trees can memorise noise; and my area-per-room ratio gave the linear model an interaction term. This is one 80/20 split with 109 test houses, so the 0.06 gap in R² is a result for this split, not a general ranking of the two methods.

06-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.heading: Mistakes I Caught and Corrected
06-mistakes-i-caught-and-corrected.text: 06 Mistakes I Caught and Corrected Unverified units: my first version labelled prices in rupees and area in square feet. The source documents neither, so I removed every currency symbol and unit, relabelled the charts "dataset units," and regenerated them. A check that could not fail: my test for leftover text columns used select_dtypes(include='object'), which returns nothing under pandas 3.0 string types even if strings remain. I replaced it with select_dtypes(exclude='number'). A heatmap title that contradicted its colours: the title said green means positive and red negative, but the palette has no red. I corrected the title and regenerated the chart. Paths that only worked from one folder: the notebook failed when launched from the repository root. I resolve the project root with pathlib so it runs from either folder. Documentation drift: an early README listed files that did not exist and described an outlier check I never ran, and the notebook summary called regression results "accuracy" and left out RMSE. I rewrote both to match the repository and report MAE, RMSE and R² together. Unpinned libraries: the saved models were serialised with specific library versions, so I pinned those versions in requirements.txt.

08-limitations-and-next-steps.heading: Limitations and Next Steps
08-limitations-and-next-steps.text: 08 Limitations and Next Steps The data is 545 houses and a single 80/20 split with 109 test houses, so scores depend on the split and the gap between the two models is small. Price and area have no documented unit, and the data has no location, age, build quality or market conditions, so about a third of the variation in price (R² 0.66) is left unexplained. Both models underpredict the most expensive houses, and both give point estimates only, with no prediction intervals. Two engineered features are exact sums of existing columns, so the design matrix has rank 14 of 16. Predictions are unaffected, but individual linear coefficients share weight and should not be read one by one. Everything here is association; no claim about cause is made. Next steps: repeated cross-validation for both models to test whether the gap holds, a log-transformed target, and prediction intervals.
